t: Minimum Adjacent Swaps to Reach the Kth Smallest Number — Editorial
o: A wonderful integer is any permutation of the digits of num that is strictly greater than num; ranked increasingly, we must reach the k-th one with the fewest adjacent swaps. Successively greater permutations are produced by the classic next-permutation transformation, so the k-th smallest wonderful number is simply num after k applications — from "5489355142", four applications give "5489355421", matching the example list. The remaining question is the minimum adjacent swaps between the ORIGINAL string and that target. With duplicated digits the rule is: scan the target left to right and always pull the LEFTMOST still-unused matching digit of the source, bubbling it into place; in the example that costs 1 + 1 = 2 swaps. Length and k are at most 1000, so an O(k*n) generation plus an O(n^2) count is comfortably fast.
k: The k-th smallest wonderful number is exactly num after applying the standard next-permutation step k times.
Minimum adjacent swaps between two arrangements of one multiset: each target position takes the LEFTMOST unused matching source digit; the bubble distances sum to the optimum.
Do not accumulate swaps while stepping through the k permutations — measure the distance between the start array and the final array.

a.n: Approach 1: Next Permutation k Times + Physical Bubble Counting
a.i: Generate the target by running next permutation k times on a digit array. Then replay the transformation greedily on a copy of the original: for each target position, find the nearest matching digit at or after the cursor and bubble it left with adjacent swaps, counting each exchange. Physically performing the swaps proves achievability, and leftmost matching proves minimality.
s: Copy digits into an array; repeat k times: find the rightmost ascent i, swap digits[i] with the smallest strictly larger digit to its right, reverse the suffix after i.
Scan the target and source arrays with index i from left to right.
When they disagree at i, locate the wanted digit at j > i and bubble it to position i, adding j - i to the answer.
Return the accumulated count when all positions agree.
a.t: O(k*n + n^2) — k linear next-permutation passes plus a quadratic greedy count; fine for n, k <= 1000

a.n: Approach 2: Next Permutation + Fenwick Tree Displacement Counting
a.i: Replace the physical bubbling with inversion counting. Process target positions left to right, take the leftmost UNUSED source position holding the needed digit, and add the number of still-unused positions to its left — precisely what bubbling would have cost. A Fenwick tree over source positions (1 = unused) answers both "how many unused before p" and "mark p used" in O(log n), while per-digit ascending position lists with one pointer each supply the leftmost unused occurrence.
s: Build the target with k next-permutation passes as before.
Bucket original positions by digit in ascending order; keep one pointer per digit.
For each target digit, advance that pointer past used cells to its leftmost unused position p.
Add the count of unused positions before p to the answer, then clear p in the BIT.
a.t: O(k*n + n log n) — generation dominates; counting costs only logarithmic work per matched digit
a.sp: O(n) — BIT, digit buckets, and pointers

w: Present the next-permutation reduction first; it is the crux of the problem. The classic mistake is summing swaps while performing each of the k transformations: for num = "132" and k = 2 the true answer is 3, yet naively accumulating per-step costs gives 4 — always measure start-to-finish. Duplicated digits are handled by the leftmost-unused matching rule, which keeps relative order stable and the count provably minimal. Follow-ups: k up to 10^9 or beyond (construct the k-th permutation directly with factorial numbering), or outputting the actual swap sequence.
